title: Silencing hepatic complement factor B inhibits alternative pathway activation and attenuates arthritis in CAIA model
abstract: The complement system comprises tightly regulated enzymatic cascades that are essential for innate immune defense and tissue homeostasis. Although protective under physiological conditions, complement dysregulation can drive inflammation and tissue injury and contributes to the pathogenesis of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, prompting the development of complement-targeted therapies. Here, we describe the development and nonclinical evaluation of AZD6912, a GalNAc-conjugated small interfering RNA (siRNA) designed to silence hepatic complement factor B ( CFB ) as a potential treatment for rheumatoid arthritis. AZD6912 produced potent on-target knockdown of CFB in a hepatocyte cell line and a primary human hepatocyte spheroid model, with no evidence of off-target effects. In mice, a surrogate siRNA targeting hepatic Cfb achieved >90% reduction in liver Cfb mRNA and >95% reduction in circulating CFB protein. This target-specific silencing reduced local complement production, attenuated joint inflammation, and provided therapeutic benefit in the collagen antibody-induced arthritis (CAIA) model. In non-human primates, AZD6912 showed high hepatic exposure, >80% suppression of hepatic CFB mRNA, sustained reductions in serum CFB, and >95% inhibition of complement activity. Safety assessments were unremarkable. Collectively, these findings demonstrate durable siRNA-mediated silencing of CFB with downstream pharmacologic and therapeutic effects, support the clinical development of AZD6912, and highlight the potential of GalNAc-siRNA therapeutics in immune-mediated diseases.

title: Selection and characterization of ssDNA aptamers targeting tick-borne encephalitis virus particles
abstract: Aptamers are single-stranded nucleic acids that bind to target molecules with high affinity, serving as versatile molecular tools for diagnostic and therapeutic applications. Although several aptamers against the envelope (E) protein of tick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV) have been reported, their recognition of native viral particles remain insufficiently characterized. We identified novel ssDNA aptamers against TBEV through systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) using a recombinant E protein that preserved the major antigenic properties of viral particles. The four major aptamer candidates showed binding activity not only to TBEV E proteins but also to TBEV-derived subviral particles. Additionally, these aptamers recognized TBEV-infected cells and retained their binding activity under serum conditions mimicking the in vivo environment. Some aptamers also exhibited inhibitory effects against TBEV infection in vitro . Furthermore, sequence truncation yielded optimized variants that retained high target affinity, demonstrated enhanced serum stability over 24 h, and neutralized viral infection. These findings provide crucial functional validation of ssDNA aptamers targeting TBEV particles and support their development as antibody-independent platforms for diagnostic, antiviral, and targeted delivery strategies for TBEV and related flaviviruses.

title: Preclinical sustained analgesia and translational potential of AAV-encoded CaV3.2 peptide aptamers for peripherally targeted pain therapy
abstract: We previously identified two calcium channel 3.2 (Ca V 3.2) inhibitory peptide aptamers (3.2iPA1 and 3.2iPA2) for adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated, sensory neuron-targeted analgesia in rat pain models. This study investigated the long-term preclinical analgesic efficacy of AAV-Ca V 3.2iPAs and translational potential by assessing their effects in human sensory neurons. We generated AAV6.2FF-encoded concatemeric 3.2iPA (Co3.2iPA), comprising 3.2iPA1 and 3.2iPA2 in tandem. Analgesic efficacy was assessed by injecting AAV6.2FF-Co3.2iPA into the lumbar dorsal root ganglion (DRG) of rats with tibial nerve injury (TNI)-induced painful neuropathy. Results showed that pain behaviors were relieved for 4 months of observation, with magnitudes and time courses comparable between male and female TNI rats. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and AAV genome analysis confirmed the peripheral nerve-restricted biodistribution of Co3.2iPA and long-term transgene expression. Co3.2iPA inhibited T-type calcium channels and suppressed action potential firing in human sensory neurons, supporting the translational potential of AAV6.2FF-Co3.2iPA delivery to the DRG for treating intractable chronic pain conditions resistant to current therapies.

title: Targeting cryptic splicing variants in SDCCAG8, CEP290, and ABCA4: A translational workflow from diagnosis to ASO-based therapy
abstract: A definitive molecular diagnosis is essential for the clinical management of rare genetic diseases (RGDs), guiding prognosis, genetic counseling, and therapeutic development. RNA-based therapeutics have emerged as promising strategies for RGDs owing to their ability to modulate gene expression and splicing. Here, we establish an integrated and scalable pipeline from variant discovery to RNA-based therapy in inherited retinal diseases (IRDs). Genome sequencing identified three cryptic variants in known IRD genes. Two novel deep intronic variants in SDCCAG8 were characterized by RT-PCR to induce pseudoexon inclusion. In addition, a previously described deep intronic variant in CEP290 was detected and reproduced on patient-derived fibroblasts, confirming aberrant splicing. A third family carrying the recurrent ABCA4 c.768G>T silent variant was included to corroborate the translational strength of our pipeline and to provide an additional model for RNA-based therapeutic correction. We designed and tested 16 splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides (ssASOs) in patient-derived fibroblasts, HeLa cells transfected with mutant minigenes, and, when available, human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal organoids. For each variant, at least one ssASO successfully improved normal splicing and increased gene expression in patient-derived models. Overall, this study validates an innovative end-to-end translational workflow and highlights how molecular diagnosis can directly drive the development of personalized RNA-based therapies.

Polymeric Nanoparticles for a Localized In Vivo Production of Therapeutic Antibodies
abstract: The local production of therapeutic proteins has generated considerable interest in the research community as a strategy to overcome the challenges associated with conventional protein-based therapies, such as high costs, the inconvenience of repeated administrations, and unwanted side effects. This review explores the potential of targeted polymeric nanoparticles that carry nucleic acids to induce controlled, localized production of therapeutic antibodies. Polymeric nanoparticles are analyzed on the basis of four key components: i) the polymer matrix, including cationic, non- cationic, lipid-polymer hybrid, and cyclodextrin-based systems; ii) the genetic payload designed for antibody production; iii) linker chemistry, ranging from standard covalent bonds to stimuli- responsive or non-covalent bonds; and iv) potential targeting tools such as antibodies/fragments, peptides, or aptamers, for identifying target cells. By combining gene therapy with nanomedicine, these particles reduce immune responses and show great promise for treating cancer, infections, and autoimmune diseases. To this end, their structure is discussed in relation to the therapeutic antibody’s mechanism of action, and to their in vivo validation as a next-generation platform for antibody-based immunotherapies.

title: Re-entering the cell: Is the intracellular space the true therapeutic niche for aptamers?
abstract: First conceptualized in the early 1990s by the Tuerk, Gold, and Szostak laboratories, nucleic acid aptamers—often dubbed “chemical antibodies”—were envisioned as a disruptive class of targeted therapeutics.1 Selected via systemic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX), an iterative in vitro process that sorts massive combinatorial libraries for high-affinity sequences, aptamers fold into distinct tertiary structures capable of binding to protein targets with nanomolar or sub-nanomolar dissociation constants.

title: Controlling the controls: On the importance of validated negative control ASOs
abstract: Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapeutics have moved from a niche modality to a validated class of drugs, with more than a dozen agents now approved and many more advancing through preclinical and clinical pipelines. Each of these programs depends on a deceptively simple ingredient: a negative control ASO that separates the sequence-specific activity of a candidate oligonucleotide from the effects of its chemistry and delivery. In practice, researchers usually improvise a scrambled or mismatched control for each new candidate, an approach that is rarely well characterized and can involve unpredictable biological activity.

abstract: Better treatments are urgently needed for eye conditions when existing therapies fall short. Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a significant contributor to irreversible central vision impairment in an aging population. The neovascular form of AMD (nAMD) accounts for most severe vision loss due to choroidal neovascularization (CNV), a process often leading to subretinal hemorrhage, photoreceptor cell death, and ultimately permanent fibrovascular scarring.1 At present, standard treatments use recombinant anti-VEGF fusion proteins or antibodies injected intravitreally every few months.

title: Beyond repressor disruption: Designing activator motifs to boost fetal hemoglobin
abstract: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) reactivation is now a powerful and clinically validated strategy for sickle cell disease (SCD). Many genome-editing approaches achieve this by disrupting regulatory sequences involved in γ-globin silencing, such as the BCL11A erythroid enhancer. In a recent issue of Molecular Therapy Nucleic Acids, Chalumeau et al.1 replaced the BCL11A binding site in the HBG1/2 promoters with a composite TAL1:GATA1 activating motif rather than only disrupting a repressor site. The edited promoters supported robust γ-globin expression and reduced sickling in erythroid cells derived from SCD hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs).

title: Development of a G-Quadruplex-Forming DNA Aptamer Against EGFR-Driven Malignancies
abstract: Abstract BACKGROUND Cancer remains a major cause of mortality globally, and EGFR overexpression is implicated in ~30% of epithelial malignancies with poor prognosis. While two classes of drugs are clinically approved for their treatment, these drugs suffer from drawbacks, including acquired resistance, bypassed signalling, limited solid tumor penetration, on-target toxicity, and higher production costs. To overcome these limitations, we require alternative therapeutics against the EGFR altered cancers. METHODS In this study, we identified Apt64, a novel G-quadruplex-forming DNA aptamer, using Protein-SELEX against a baculovirus-expressed EGFR ectodomain. Biophysical and biochemical analysis of Apt64 revealed the formation of a stable parallel G-quadruplex conformation, exceptional thermal and serum stability. Functional assays were performed with different cancer cell lines to evaluate target specificity, cytotoxicity, cell cycle analysis, apoptosis assay, and inhibition of EGFR signalling RESULTS The selected aptamer exhibited high-affinity binding for sEGFR ( Kd = 25.77 nM), comparable to Cetuximab ( Kd = 8.98 nM). Functional evaluation in different cell lines suggested its target specificity and superior efficacy compared to Cetuximab. Apt64 induced 83% G0/G1 cell cycle arrest at 250 nM, whereas Cetuximab caused only 67% arrest even at 500 nM and triggered more than two-fold higher apoptosis than Cetuximab. Further, Apt64 effectively inhibited EGFR phosphorylation at Tyr1068, thereby stalling downstream signalling required for cancer cell survival and proliferation. CONCLUSIONS Collectively, these findings highlight Apt64 as a potent, structurally stable, and cost-effective therapeutic candidate against EGFR-driven cancers compared with existing therapies, warranting further preclinical and clinical evaluation.

abstract: Aptamers are emerging as versatile tools in cancer research and therapy because they combine high target specificity with low immunogenicity, chemical tractability, and straightforward sequence optimization. They have been developed for tumor recognition, biomarker detection, targeted delivery of drugs and therapeutic RNAs, and direct modulation of oncogenic or immune pathways.1,2 Their programmable nature also creates opportunities to target intracellular protein interactions that remain largely inaccessible to conventional therapeutics.

title: Paloma Giangrande appointed for a second term as the editor-in-chief of Molecular Therapy Nucleic Acids
abstract: Dr. Giangrande, an internationally recognized RNA pioneer and executive with over 20 years of expertise across academia and industry, has been appointed for a second term as editor-in-chief of Molecular Therapy Nucleic Acids (MTNA). She has served as editor-in-chief since 2022, and her second five-year term will begin in January 2027. During her first term, she guided MTNA through an era of unprecedented growth in nucleic acid therapeutics. Under her leadership, the journal expanded its scope to include computational biology and AI/machine-learning applications.

title: PIWIL2: A new link between RNA biology, inflammation, and ischemic brain injury
abstract: Ischemic stroke begins with a sudden interruption of blood flow to the brain, but the damage does not stop when blood flow is restored. The initial ischemic insult triggers a series of secondary events, including inflammation, oxidative stress, cell death, and disrupted genomic regulation. These can continue to damage the brain well beyond the initial vascular event. Mapping the molecular pathways that link ischemic stress to this secondary injury remains one of the persistent challenges in stroke research.

title: Therapeutic silencing of serine/threonine kinase 25 for obesity-associated MASLD
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is projected to affect 38% of adults and is now the leading cause of chronic liver disease worldwide.1 MASLD spans a continuum from simple steatosis to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), which can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The only FDA-approved therapies for patients with MASH and moderate-to-advanced fibrosis are semaglutide and resmetirom, an oral, liver-directed, thyroid hormone receptor β (THR-β)-selective agonist.

title: Beyond lysosomal storage: Correcting Fabry cardiomyocyte dysfunction with modified GLA mRNA
abstract: Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic variants in GLA, resulting in deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme α-galactosidase A (α-Gal A) and progressive accumulation of glycosphingolipids, particularly globotriaosylceramide (Gb3). Cardiac involvement is a major determinant of morbidity and mortality in Fabry disease. However, the cellular mechanisms linking the primary defect of α-Gal A deficiency and lysosomal storage to cardiomyocyte dysfunction remain incompletely understood.

abstract: As a monogenic disorder, cystic fibrosis (CF) has long been viewed as an attractive candidate for a one-size-fits-all gene therapy approach. Combined with the fact that the most clinically relevant target cells are located within the human airway epithelium (HAE), which was once thought to be readily accessible through aerosolized vector delivery, CF appeared to be the ideal disease for targeted gene therapy development. However, except for two currently ongoing studies, all clinical trials for viral vector-mediated, lung-targeted CFTR gene therapy have been stopped in their tracks before phase 3.

title: Machine learning-guided design of artificial microRNAs for targeted gene silencing
abstract: Abstract Artificial microRNAs (amiRNAs) offer a powerful strategy for targeted gene silencing, but their rational design is limited by complex sequence-structure-processing relationships and the lack of tools capable of optimizing efficacy and specificity. To address this need, we developed miRarchitect, a web-based platform that uses machine learning to support the customizable design of amiRNAs. miRarchitect integrates neural network-guided target-site selection, siRNA insert design, and scaffold choice, utilizing large-scale data from human primary microRNAs (pri-miRNAs) and next-generation sequencing. The platform generates molecules that closely resemble endogenous pri-miRNAs and includes comprehensive off-target analysis to enhance specificity. Experimental validation targeting TMPRSS2 and ACE-2 confirmed precise processing, robust knockdown, and high specificity of miRarchitect-designed amiRNAs. In comparative benchmarking, miRarchitect consistently produced functional amiRNAs, whereas only half of the top candidates generated by other tools showed measurable activity. miRarchitect is freely available at https://rnadrug.ichb.pl/mirarchitect and provides an intuitive interface with an automated workflow for generating, ranking, and selecting candidate amiRNAs for research and therapeutic applications.
